paragraphs: §0 — Bab 3 tail (§§15-16): conclusion of the parity-of-acts argument

[p301, the continuation of Bab 3 §15 — "if He created justice and was thereby just, and writing and was thereby a writer, and benefaction and was thereby a benefactor"] — it is said to him: It also does not follow that by creating death He becomes dead, even if by creating speech He becomes a speaker.

§16. Then it is said to him: Do you claim that God's speech is an attribute (ṣifa) belonging to Him in His essence, and is not an act of His acts? If he says: Yes — it is said to him: Then say also that the Book is an attribute belonging to Him in His essence, and is not an act of His acts. If he says: The Book cannot be other than an act — it is said to him: The same applies to the Speech. And whatever ground he relies on to establish that the Book is created, the like of it binds him for the Speech, with no distinction between them. This is what the place [in this argument] can bear in this matter. And now we return to what we were on — the matter of the Christians.

: The closing formula wa-l-ān naʿūd ilā mā kunnā fīhi min amr al-naṣārā ("and now we return to what we were on, the matter of the Christians") is structurally important: it marks the end of the Ibn Kullāb digression of Bab 3 and frames Bab 4 as a return to the anti-Christian polemic proper. The point of the digression was to show that the qidam al-kalima apparatus refutes Christianity and Sunni kalām al-nafsī with a single demonstration; the point of returning is to address the next layer of Christian apologetic — the sirr-defense.
§1 — First refutation: if you can demonstrate the Trinity now, the earlier prophets could have demonstrated it then
So it is said to them: Tell us — is there a demonstrative proof (dalīl) for the claim that the Creator is one jawhar with three aqānīm, or not?

They must necessarily concede that they have a proof for this, since it is not admissible to affirm what there is no proof for. And since they, on their own view, do indeed demonstrate this from both the rational and the scriptural [evidence], it is said to them: Then the very existence of a demonstration for this is a refutation of what you claim — namely, that the people who preceded were not made privy to this. For if they were possessed of intellects and cognitions (dhawū ʿuqūl wa-maʿārif) by which they knew unseen matters [p300] such as the createdness of the world (ḥadath al-ʿālam) and the affirmation of the Maker (ithbāt al-ṣāniʿ) through rational proofs (al-barāhīn al-ʿaqliyya), then they ought to have inferred what you claim — that the Creator is one jawhar with three aqānīm — by the very demonstration which proved it to you. For just as it is established for them, and they inferred the createdness of the world and the affirmation of God the Creator (sublime be His praise) and His unity, from what we [now] infer from — namely, that the bodies in which is the affair of composition, and the accidents which prove to us that they are temporally-originated and that they have an Originator who originated them — these very things proved the like to them.

And as for your claim that the demonstration is that He is living and knowing (ḥayy ʿālim): they were knowers that He is living and knowing, [too — by the same proofs we now use]. But if they were not knowers of that, but were rather aimless (sudā) without intellect or cognition, then this statement suffices [to disgrace its sayer] — and the disgrace (faḍīḥa) of its sayer is manifest.

Moreover, you claim a demonstration for what you say from the Scripture and from the statement of the preceding prophets. So how can it be admissible that the preceding prophets said things proving that the Creator is one jawhar with three aqānīm — and yet they themselves did not know that what they said proved that? Can there be in the absurd, the impudent, and the brazen anything more than this?

: The argument is a classic qiyās al-ʿaql-move: the cognitive faculties of Moses, Abraham, and the other Hebrew prophets are no different in kind from those of the Christian theologians, and the demonstrative apparatus is the same. The implicit philosophical commitment — that rational demonstration is universally available to ūlū al-albāb (the people of intellect) — is again Muʿtazilī (and aligned with the ahl al-ʿadl mentioned in Bab 3 §9). The Christian sirr-defense rests on a stratification of rational capacity by historical period, which Q regards as obviously absurd: God created the same intellect for all humans, and there is no good reason why Abraham should be epistemically inferior to a Greek-trained Antiochene theologian.

: Q catches the Christian apologetic in a dilemma: either earlier scripture does not prove the Trinity (in which case the Christian appeal to it fails), or it does prove the Trinity (in which case the earlier prophets must have known, which contradicts the sirr-thesis). The dilemma was a kalāmī commonplace by Q's day but its application to progressive-revelation specifically may be a Karaite innovation — at least, it is not paralleled in the surviving Bahshamī anti-Christian materials.
§2 — Second refutation: by your parity, there could be five or ten hypostases revealed to a future generation — and why didn't God give Moses' generation the intellect to know His true essence?

It is also said to them: Is not the truth of the essence (ḥaqīqat dhāt) of the Creator that He is one jawhar, three aqānīm? Every one of the people who preceded the coming of Jesus knew that He is a jawhar, but did not know that He is three aqānīm; this was not disclosed to them because their intellects could not reach it and could not bear it. If they say: Yes — it is said to them: Then how is it secured (mā yuʾmanu) that He has other attributes (ṣifāt ukhar) and additional aqānīm beyond these — five, or ten — that were not disclosed to those of the age of Jesus, because their intellects could not bear it, and only that much of it was disclosed to them as their intellects reached? — just as no more than [bare] unity (al-waḥdāniyya) was disclosed to those of the age of Moses, and the matter of the aqānīm was not disclosed to them, because their intellects did not reach it and could not bear it. And it may be admissible that another people arise whose intellects can bear it, and the matter of the [further] aqānīm is disclosed to them, just as the matter of the three aqānīm was disclosed to the companions of Jesus.

And further: if God is the One who created people and created intellects for them, then why did He create great creation from the time of Adam until Jesus came [yet] not create for them intellects by which they might attain the knowledge of the truth of His essence [p299] — among whom were many prophets? Is this not nothing but sukhna ʿayn of a statement — does its ugliness and corruption escape even the beasts, let alone the people of intellect?

: The "parity reduction to 5 or 10 hypostases" is Q's sharpest move in the bab. The sirr-defense, taken seriously, has no internal stopping rule: if God can disclose 3-hypostases to one generation while withholding it from earlier ones, He can disclose 5 or 10 to a later generation while withholding it from us. The Christian apologist either accepts the conclusion (and grants that future Christians may correctly reject the Trinitarian definitions of Nicaea-Constantinople in favor of a 5- or 10-hypostatic theology) or rejects the sirr-defense itself. The same parity reductio is preserved in SUK 5426-5429, deployed not against the sirr-defense but against the Christian Trinity-as-attribute-theology fallback: wa-baʿd, fa-inna hādhihi al-ṭarīqa tūjib ʿalaykum an tazīdū fī ʿadad al-aqānīm bi-ʿadad ṣifātihi jalla wa-ʿazz, wa-an tuthbitū lahu uqnūman bi-kawnihi qādiran, wa-uqnūman bi-kawnihi ʿāliman, wa-ākhar bi-kawnihi mudrikan, wa-rābiʿan wa-khāmisan bi-kawnihi murīdan wa-kārihan ḥattā yablugha ʿadad al-aqānīm thamāniya aw tisʿa, wa-qad ʿurifa fasāduhu ("further: this method of yours requires you to increase the number of hypostases by the number of His attributes, mighty and exalted — and to posit a hypostasis for His being-qādir, a hypostasis for His being-ʿālim, another for His being-mudrik, a fourth and a fifth for His being-murīd and kārih — until the number of hypostases reaches eight or nine. The absurdity of this is well-known"). Q's deployment of the parity reductio targets the sirr-as-progressive-revelation gambit; the Bahshamī deployment targets the aqānīm-as-attributes gambit; but the inferential pattern (open-ended doctrinal escalation via parity) is identical. Q likely takes the move directly from the Bahshamī polemical handbook (the school of Abū Hāshim al-Jubbāʾī, d. 321/933) and redeploys it against a Christian apologetic move ʿAbd al-Jabbār does not separately address. The "5 or 10" / "8 or 9" specific numerals are arbitrary — both authors are signaling "there is no principled stopping rule." See [[glossary]] s.v. aqānīm, ṣifāt.

: Sukhna ʿayn (literally "fever of the eye") is a robust Arabic colloquialism, often translated "miserable wretched [talk]" or "what a piece of nonsense" — a register Q rarely descends to. The signal is that he regards the sirr-defense as an embarrassment.
§3 — Third refutation: the Christian denigration of Torah law is refuted by their own Gospel — Matthew 5:17 and Mark 2:23

As for their statement that the commandments of the Torah are not chosen, not pleasing (ghayr mukhtāra wa-lā marḍiyya), but were rather imposed in anger (dufiʿat ʿalā sakhaṭ) — we have no need to lengthen [the discussion] of refuting it. For the intellects and the elite (al-ʿuqūl wa-l-khawāṣṣ) bear witness against their statement on this, as does what came of the promise (al-waʿd) by the hand of Moses (peace be upon him) and other prophets for its [the Torah's] acceptance and its adoption, and of the threat (al-waʿīd) for abandoning it and turning from it. And how is it permissible that the bewildered ones (al-ḥayārā) should say this — were it not for the excess of impudence in them — when their own book, which is the Gospel (al-Injīl), proclaims the contrary of that?

For it is written in chapter five of Mattā (Matthew) — which is the first of the four Gospels — that Yasūʿ (who is the Messiah) said [Q's Arabic of Matt 5:17, with the reference cited in his text as מת׳ ה׳, י״ז]:

And he [Jesus] said in chapter two of the Gospel of Mārqūs (Mark) [Q's text cites the reference as מרקוס ב׳, כ״ג, = Mark 2:23-26]: that Jesus was walking among the standing grain on the Sabbath day, and some of his disciples began to pluck the ears and to rub them as they walked, and the Sages (al-aḥbār) said to him: "Look at what your disciples are doing on the Sabbath, of what is not lawful!" — and Jesus answered them, saying: "Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those with him, how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the table of the Lord (khubz māʾidat al-Rabb) which was not lawful for him to eat — but only the priests may eat it?" [p298, continuing] — now if the Torah, in Jesus' view, were abolished (sāqiṭa) or not pleasing (ghayr marḍiyya), there would have been no need for him to argue against them with this argument or to apologize with this apology — rather, the greater argument would have been for him to say that this commandment, which is the Sabbath day, has fallen, become void, and passed away, since in origin it was neither pleasing nor chosen. So his leaving aside that argument and arguing with the argument he did use is the strongest proof of the falsehood of their statement.
§4 — The Christian fallback: "true" commandments are those tied to otherworldly reward/punishment, which the Torah does not mention

They sometimes cling, in support of this statement, to [the claim] that the pleasing command and prohibition (al-amr wa-l-nahy al-marḍī) are [only] those upon which is laid the promise and threat (al-waʿd wa-l-waʿīd) — namely [the promise and threat] of eternal reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb al-abadī) which does not pass away, and which obtains in the world-to-come (al-ākhira) — since the pleasures of this world and its pains are not real (ḥaqīqiyya), being severable and passing. They say: We have not seen the Torah speak of otherworldly (ākhirī) reward and punishment; it only promised and threatened with the immediate (ʿājil) reward and punishment which is in this world (al-dunyā); and that is clear in more than one place of it. So since that is so — and since the real reward and punishment is not the temporary worldly one — it is established that this obligation, upon which the real reward and punishment is not threatened, is not a pleasing obligation; the pleasing is something else.

We shall display the corruption of this dissimulation (tamwīh) which they have brought, and show the mention of the otherworldly reward and punishment from the Torah and the other books of the prophets (peace be upon them) from several places — and that [will come] after our finishing the mention of what they cite from Scripture and the refutation of it.

Moreover, if the Torah and its commandments are not pleasing and were imposed in anger — then what do they themselves mean by reading it, adopting it, studying it, and seeking its interpretation? Is this anything but self-contradiction in speech?

: Q's logical move is sharp: Jesus' grain-plucking defense (Mark 2:23-26) is a Torah-juridical move (David ate the showbread; therefore Sabbath commands admit emergency-exceptions), and a Torah-juridical move presupposes the Torah's binding force. Were Jesus an abrogationist, he would not have reached for a Torah-internal precedent — he would simply have declared the Sabbath void. The argument-form Q identifies here (call it the "argument from the form of the defense") was important in later Jewish anti-Christian polemic; it surfaces, e.g., in Profayt Duran's Kelimmat ha-Goyim (14th c.).

: A devastating ad hominem: the Christians copy the Torah, translate it, commentate on it, and treat it as canonical scripture — which is wholly inexplicable on their own thesis that it was given in anger and is not pleasing to God. The objection echoes a similar move in earlier Jewish-Christian polemic (Saadia and the Qiṣṣat Mujādalat al-Usquf tradition) but Q sharpens it into a logical contradiction-charge.

: Al-ḥayārā ("the bewildered ones") is Q's standard polemical sobriquet for the Christians — playing on what he regards as their doctrinal incoherence on the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the abrogation of Torah. He uses the term repeatedly in Maqala III; Chiesa and Lockwood 1984 render it "the perplexed" or "the muddled."

: Q's deployment of Matt 5:17 ("not one yod or stroke") and Mark 2:23-26 (the grain-plucking and the showbread) is the classical Jewish anti-Christological move: if the Gospel itself records Jesus affirming the binding force of the Torah (Matt 5:17) and reasoning within the Torah's juridical framework (Mark 2:23-26, where Jesus defends Sabbath conduct by appeal to a Torah precedent), then the Christian claim that Jesus abrogated the Torah is internally inconsistent with their own scripture. The argument is paralleled in earlier Jewish-Arabic anti-Christian literature (e.g., in the Nestor ha-Komer / Qiṣṣat Mujādalat al-Usquf recension and in Saadia's lost anti-Christian work cited by ʿAbd al-Jabbār); Q's distinctive contribution is the systematicity with which he turns the Synoptic Gospels against the Pauline-patristic abrogation-theology. Note that Q's Arabic translation of Matt 5:17 preserves the Hebraism "yāʾ wāḥida aw khaṭṭ wāḥid" ("a single yod or a single stroke") — the iota of the Greek Vorlage already half-Hebraized in Q's text. The Mark passage Q quotes is a translation of Mk 2:23-26 that compresses the ascription "ḥīna sāʾala Abyātar al-imām al-akbar" (the Abiathar / Ahimelech crux of Mk 2:26) — Q simply omits the priestly name, perhaps because of a Vorlage variant or perhaps to sidestep the difficulty.

- The architecture of Bab 4. The bab is unusually short (3 manuscript pages versus 8 for Bab 3 and ~19 for Bab 6) and tightly focused on a single Christian apologetic move: the sirr-defense, which holds that Trinitarian doctrine was progressively revealed and was not accessible to the earlier prophets. Q's three counter-arguments — the parity-of-intellect argument (§1), the parity-of-progressive-revelation argument (§2), and the internal-incoherence-of-the-Gospel argument (§3) — function as a stress-test on the sirr-thesis from three angles.

- The Christian sirr-defense. The doctrine Q is attacking is well-attested in Eastern Christian apologetic of the 9th-10th centuries. Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī (d. 974), Q's most prominent Christian contemporary, repeatedly deploys the language of sirr (mystery / arcanum) and al-fahm al-ʿālī (lofty understanding) to defend the Trinity against rationalist objections. Q's anti-sirr argumentation is the Karaite counterpart to the rationalist Muslim attacks on the same defense (e.g., in ʿAbd al-Jabbār's Mughnī Vol. 5, al-Firaq Ghayr al-Islāmiyya).

- The parity-to-five-or-ten-hypostases argument (§2). This is Q's signature move in the bab, and it has no exact parallel in the surviving Muslim or Jewish anti-Christian polemical corpus. The argument exploits the sirr-defense's lack of an internal stopping rule: if doctrine can be progressively disclosed as intellects grow, there is no principled bar against future doctrinal escalation. The Christian apologist is forced to either (i) accept that future revelation may yet disclose 5 or 10 hypostases (and thereby grant that current Christian dogma is provisional), or (ii) deny the parity, which requires a principled distinction between the closure of revelation at the Apostolic age and its earlier openness — a distinction Q presumes the Christian cannot non-arbitrarily draw.

- The Gospel-against-the-Christian argument (§3). Q's Arabic Vorlage of the Synoptic Gospels is worth noting. His Matt 5:17 quotation preserves the Hebraism "a single yāʾ or a single stroke" — pointing to a Vorlage that already half-Hebraized the Greek ἰῶτα. His Mark 2:23-26 quotation omits the famously crux-laden ascription to Abiathar (Mk 2:26 has Jesus referring to a priest who, on the standard reading of 1 Sam 21:1-7, was actually Ahimelech), which suggests either a smoothing recension or a polemically-motivated abbreviation. The Christian Arabic Gospel tradition Q is drawing on probably belongs to one of the early Arabic recensions known to us via the Sinai and Mt. Athos manuscripts (cf. Hikmat Kachouh, The Arabic Versions of the Gospels, 2012, for the recension-history).

- The "intellects and the elite" (§3, al-ʿuqūl wa-l-khawāṣṣ). The phrase appeals to a kind of consensus omnium of the rational and elite — a kalāmī-philosophical commonplace by Q's day, ultimately Aristotelian (endoxa of ta sophoi), mediated through the Bahshamī apparatus of ʿaql and fiṭra.

- What's missing. The bab does not engage the Pauline theology of the abrogation of the Torah (e.g., Galatians, Romans). Q's argument in §3 stays within the Synoptic Gospels and relies on the in-house Synoptic affirmation of Torah-bindingness. This is consistent with the broader Karaite (and Geonic-Jewish) strategy of treating Jesus as a Torah-faithful Galilean reformer whose actual teachings were systematically distorted by Paul and the patristic tradition. Q does not develop that genealogical claim explicitly here, but it is the implied background.

- For the sirr-defense in Eastern Christian apologetic: Sidney Griffith, The Church in the Shadow of the Mosque (2008), Ch. 3 on the Christian-Arabic theological literature; Mark Swanson, "Beyond Prooftexting" on the Arabic-Christian appropriation of biblical and patristic argument. - For Yaḥyā b. ʿAdī's anti-rationalist Christian apologetic: E. Platti, Yaḥyā ibn ʿAdī, théologien chrétien et philosophe arabe (1983); R.M. Frank's review-essay in JAOS 105 (1985). - For Q's deployment of the Synoptic Gospels: Daniel Lasker, Jewish Philosophical Polemics Against Christianity in the Middle Ages (2nd ed. 2007), Ch. 4 on the use of the Gospels in Karaite anti-Christian polemic, including a specific discussion of Q's Mark 2:23-26 quotation. - For the progressive revelation trope and its medieval Jewish refutation: Maud Kozodoy, "Medieval Jewish anti-Christian polemic and the progressivism defense" in Jewish History 24 (2010); Robert Chazan, Daggers of Faith (1989) on the Christian-side of the same debate in the 13th century. - For the Arabic Synoptic Vorlage Q is using: Hikmat Kachouh, The Arabic Versions of the Gospels (2012), esp. her treatment of the Sinaitic and Mt. Athos recensions; Samir Khalil Samir, "La version arabe des Évangiles" in POr 22 (1994-95). - For Matt 5:17 in medieval Jewish-Christian polemic generally: Daniel Boyarin, Border Lines (2004) on Matt 5:17 as the contested verse between Jewish and Christian self-definition; Adiel Schremer, Brothers Estranged (2010) for the Tannaitic background.
